metldr is a free AI assistant for Chrome that reads, researches and does real browser work for you, with your approval, using the AI you choose: your API keys, the coding agents you already use, or fully local models. > [!WARNING] > **Work in progress: new version.** metldr is being rebuilt in Rust with a new Rune-based interface, a native companion, and expanded browser control. Features, interfaces and data formats may change, and some parts are not finished yet. The current extension remains the reference until each replacement reaches parity. * Summarize pages, PDFs and Gmail, look up words and search pages. * Run approved tasks, restore chats, and choose APIs, installed agents or local AI. ## Planned features Some features are available today, and the full list is planned. ### Browser work and conversations * Work in your allowed signed in tabs: read pages, inspect controls and layouts, and capture screenshots. * Navigate pages, history and tabs, track new tabs and popups, and group tabs by task or conversation. * Click, double click, hover, drag, drop, scroll and select, with context menus, keyboard shortcuts and the clipboard. * Fill forms across pages, upload files, edit rich text, and run approved page scripts or WebMCP page tools. * Review plans, set scoped approval rules and automatic approvals for each session, and see when browser control is active. * Stop, pause and resume tasks, and verify results, redirects and dead links. * Keep and restore chats, attachments, live activity and interrupted results, and continue work across conversations. * Send selected content and website prompts to the sidebar, and get contextual suggestions while browsing. * Organize projects, goals and working directories. ### Tasks you can complete * Summarize pages, emails, PDFs and video transcripts, explain code, contracts and research, and create study notes and flashcards. * Triage inboxes, flag urgent messages and draft follow ups for unanswered threads. * Research companies, suppliers and products, and compare prices, quotes and sources with citations. * Find, qualify and track leads, and draft outreach and connection requests. * Complete applications and surveys from documents, and extract invoices and reconcile payments. * Screen applicants, update recruitment systems, and plan agendas, appointments and invitations. * Build recurring reports across dashboards and query BigQuery and other connected data warehouses. * Track orders, bookings and price changes. ### Workflows, Skills and memory * Teach workflows through instructions or demonstrations, and save them as versioned templates with inputs, outputs and approval rules. * Run workflows and Skills manually, through slash commands, on schedules with timezones, exceptions and overlap rules, or when a page title changes. * Pause, resume or remove scheduled work, recover missed and interrupted runs, and keep tasks running with the panel closed. * Start, track and manage tasks, exceptions and run histories from a dashboard. * Create, share and browse built in, site and plugin Skills, and import them from URLs or ZIP files. * Manage context files and editable memory: inspect, edit, disable or delete it, and scope corrections to projects or workflows. * Optionally sync memory, projects, workflows and preferences, and manage team workspaces, member access and shared or individual budgets. * Preview, edit, undo, list and remove site scripts, and run them automatically on matching pages. * Reuse learned site tools and cached prompts, add custom tools and dashboards to pages, and apply reading preferences and page shortcuts. * Receive completion alerts and approval requests. ### Files and interactive answers * Pin local files and folders to chats, and browse, read and write within approved working directories. * Edit Excel, CSV, browser spreadsheets, Google Sheets cell blocks, Word and browser documents while preserving formulas and unrelated content. * Search chats, pages, files and documents, and read large pages and files in chunks. * Use PDF text, OCR and dictionary lookup, and preview, zoom and navigate PDFs, images and generated files. * Attach files, clipboard images and selected text, and copy images between allowed websites. * Get streamed answers with tables, charts, diagrams, calculators, maps, interactive explanations and local controls, and save them as reusable artifacts. * Keep screenshot history during long tasks, record approved task videos for replay, and export results with screenshots or print them to PDF. * Download all task outputs together, or folders as ZIP files. ### Email, voice and remote control * Draft, reply, forward and send Gmail, and verify sent mail and approval outcomes. * Read, search and manage WhatsApp chats: send approved messages, files and reactions, manage members, roles and invite links, and control read status and history. * Dictate prompts, and review, edit or cancel voice recordings and transcripts. * Send tasks, voice notes, photos and files through Telegram or WhatsApp, and receive results, screenshots and status updates. * Approve or cancel remote actions, pair, switch and revoke devices or profiles, and let authorized MCP clients control tasks. ### Model choice and reliability * Choose popular APIs, custom endpoints, local and browser models, or approved local and network model servers, using API keys, supported account sign ins, or no key where supported. * Run Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Claude Code with their accounts, tools, permissions and sessions, and connect remote MCP servers and tools. * Switch models with visible capability limits, set timeouts and connection settings, and choose separate speech and task providers. * Inspect token usage and estimated costs, manage context with /compact and /usage, and select browser profiles through a CLI. * Recover connections without silent provider switching, and review uncertain writes before any repeat attempt. * Keep site, tab and file permissions explicit, isolate generated answers from browser authority, and keep local inference local unless you approve. * See model data destinations and access limits, with bounded storage, memory and background work. * Export, delete and recover saved data, preserved through upgrades and interrupted work. * Use multilingual and accessible controls with themes, text size and sound preferences. * Use Chrome, Edge, Brave and Chromebooks with Linux, Windows and macOS companions, and every feature without an app subscription. See the [feature guide](docs/features.md) for current availability, planned details and compatibility limits. # Claude Code session

This crate runs the installed Claude Code CLI as a MetLDR agent. It starts `claude -p` with stream-json input and output, gives it only the MCP servers MetLDR names (`--strict-mcp-config`), and routes every permission prompt back to MetLDR over stdio (`--permission-prompt-tool stdio`), so the user approves each tool use in MetLDR. New sessions get a MetLDR-chosen UUID and follow-ups resume it.

The crate never installs, signs in or pays for anything. It uses the user's own Claude Code login, or an endpoint given through `Launch::env`. Lines are bounded at 4 MiB, closing ends input and kills the process after 5 seconds, and dropping a session kills it.

The check in `tests/claude.rs` drives the installed binary against a loopback Messages fixture, so it makes no network or paid request. It is skipped when Claude Code is not installed.

# metldr companion

The companion runs provider requests, installed agents and browser tasks for the [Rust panel](../metldr-panel/README.md). It keeps run state, approvals and recovery in one native process. Browser commands use the normal Chromiumoxide dependency and the extension's debugger bridge.

Page summaries and questions have a separate text path for configured Messages, Responses, Google Interactions and Chat Completions endpoints. The request contains the saved page and completed text answers from the same page and provider selection. It offers no browser tools. Changing the provider, model or connection revision starts a separate history. The companion keeps at most six prior turns and removes whole oldest turns when the context limit is reached. It refuses a source and question that cannot fit without truncation.

Responses page questions can also produce validated tables. Tables are saved separately and reopen inside chat. They cannot run code or perform browser actions.

Text results use the same local run storage, streaming, Stop and restart handling. Partial output can remain after failure or cancellation. A native restart interrupts an active request and does not send it again. Stop closes the local stream; remote inference and billing cancellation depend on the provider.

Pi receives the shared browser tools through a temporary MCP registration for each run. Pi loads its native skills, and skill prompts receive the saved page and browser rules. Its installed tools, authentication and saved session remain under Pi control. Browser field changes use the same separate metldr approval as other execution routes. The registration file contains no endpoint secret and is removed after Pi exits. An uncertain action or unconfirmed release blocks that session from continuing automatically.

Pi extensions can request selection, confirmation, input and editor dialogs in the panel. Native notices, status, widgets, titles and editor suggestions are also shown. Dialog replies return the exact selected value or entered text. Suggestions require an explicit action before replacing the composer draft. Native timeouts remove expired controls; the companion adds no editor timeout. Stop or loss of the native controller retires pending dialogs. Native UI content and replies stay in bounded memory and are discarded when the companion restarts. Browser action approvals remain separate. Custom TUI components that Pi does not expose through RPC remain unavailable. Initial startup dialogs are rejected before showing a reply control. Installed Pi 1.3.0 does not consume replies while an extension awaits a dialog in its first `session_start` hook. Defer that dialog until after startup.

Codex and OpenCode share the panel's approval view. Codex requests can cover commands, file changes and additional permissions. Review the complete details before choosing an option. Saved command rules and session grants have separate labels. A changed file patch replaces its review and invalidates the old choice. The shared approval view is limited to 8192 encoded bytes. Larger reviews stop the task without approval. A native event backlog that prevents checking a queued decision also stops the task without applying that decision. Each agent retains its own policy and response format.

During active Codex or Pi work, use the composer to send a correction without starting another session. Stop remains available. Saved receipts distinguish native acceptance, Pi queue admission, extension handling and uncertain delivery. None confirms model use. An uncertain correction blocks session reuse and is never sent again automatically. Each run accepts at most 16 corrections of 1024 UTF8 bytes each.

Active Pi, Codex and OpenCode turns have no overall companion time limit. Startup, RPC, browser operations and resource limits still apply. After Stop is observed, the companion waits up to 15 seconds for native confirmation between protocol operations, then enters cleanup if confirmation is missing. Expiry is a failure, not confirmed cancellation. Native RPC and process cleanup retain their own deadlines. Codex and OpenCode approval prompts wait for your decision or Stop. MCP browser calls have a cumulative 30 second queue and execution limit. A saved browser approval pauses that limit until your decision or Stop. Clients that request progress and accept SSE receive updates during review. Their own request limits still apply.

Browser inspection and field changes run in a named isolated world. Page scripts cannot replace the JavaScript properties used to read or change a field. The companion still checks the current frame and execution context before using an approved action, and requests no universal access for the isolated world. A verified field value does not establish that a website accepted or saved it.

From the repository root, run:

```sh
make check-companion
make companion
```

The default output is `crates/metldr-companion/target/release/metldr-companion`. Cargo uses `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` instead when it is set. The checks write their local artifacts under this crate's `.tmp` directory.

Run the explicit history load workload with:

```sh
METLDR_HISTORY_LOAD_SCALE=1000 METLDR_HISTORY_LOAD_LAYOUT=spread METLDR_HISTORY_LOAD_BYTES=1024 \
  cargo test --locked --release --manifest-path crates/metldr-companion/Cargo.toml \
  history::load_checks::history_load_real_relationships -- --exact --ignored --nocapture --test-threads=1
```

Scale accepts `1`, `10`, `100` or `1000`. Layout accepts `spread` for separate conversations or `fanout` for one conversation. Payload size accepts `128`, `1024` or `8192` bytes. The defaults are scale `1`, layout `spread` and `1024` bytes.

Each group creates one source, 25 runs, three native workflows, three rejected browser actions and 12 table or chart artifacts through the normal storage methods. The workload checks related row counts and query results. It creates a fresh database under this crate's `.tmp` directory and removes it when the test finishes.

The `METLDR_HISTORY_LOAD_JSON` output reports seeding, reopen validation and ten query families. Each query has a first access, three warmups and 30 further observations. Query timings include validation and transaction setup and close. Reopen validation does not imply a cold operating system cache. Use independent paired processes for performance comparisons; observations within one process are correlated. Browser navigation, unfinished runs and legacy IndexedDB need separate workloads.

Process checks that require companion executables are ignored by default. To run the current startup checks on Linux or macOS, build the executable and provide its full path:

```sh
cargo build --locked --manifest-path crates/metldr-companion/Cargo.toml
METLDR_STARTUP_BINARY="$PWD/crates/metldr-companion/target/debug/metldr-companion" \
  cargo test --locked --manifest-path crates/metldr-companion/Cargo.toml \
  history::startup_checks -- --ignored --skip actual_old_private_host_upgrades_and_cannot_reopen_new_history
```

Use the actual output path if `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` is set. The two older executable compatibility checks also require fixture binaries. `METLDR_CUTOVER_OLD_BINARY` must name the earlier wire 9 companion that writes saved schema 8. `METLDR_HISTORY_OLD_BINARY` must name a companion that writes history format 10 through 18. Set `METLDR_HISTORY_EXPECT_FORMAT` to require a specific old format. The format 16 check also reads an independently prepared saved table through both executables. Run those checks explicitly with `--ignored` only when the matching fixtures are available. A skipped compatibility check does not establish upgrade support.

Pair the executable with an extension built from the same revision. The remaining Vue page tools and complete extension packaging are still being migrated. Linux is the verified native platform. On macOS the companion checks pass on APFS, including crash recovery at each history migration phase, but Chrome registration and power loss have not been tested. The history loader refuses to start on Windows until its directory durability and installation checks are complete.

Conversations and complete saved results are stored in a local record database. Startup preserves the original snapshot backup before installing the new format. New chat creates an empty conversation, while selecting a saved conversation restores its page and results. Switching is unavailable during active work. A lost confirmation requires an explicit Retry using the same request rather than another creation. Viewing saved work does not change or replay an active task. History search covers the loaded conversation pages, and More loads the next page.

Saved native sessions remain selectable after a model task and browser restart. The chooser shows up to 16 recent sessions for each agent, saved page and current profile in the selected conversation. Earlier results stay in saved history. History format 19 adds typed run and source headers so lists can read small fields without decoding complete results. It upgrades formats 10 through 18 in one transaction, preserving saved tables and complete results. Older companions refuse the upgraded history. Keep a copy of the history database before downgrading.

Register the companion with `metldr-companion install <extension id or unpacked extension directory>`. It copies the executable to `~/.local/share/metldr/bin`, writes the adjacent `metldr-companion.json` with the extension origin and a private state directory, and saves the `io.metldr.first_flow` host manifest for every installed Chrome, Chromium, Brave and Edge. The companion checks the origin Chrome supplies against that configuration and keeps a separate state directory for each browser profile. `metldr-companion uninstall` unregisters it and keeps saved history.

Provider keys stay in the native credential store. Installed agents keep their own authentication. Configure the desired provider or agent through the paired Rust panel before starting work. An action that loses confirmation remains uncertain and is not repeated automatically.

If an action request ends before its browser command is queued, the companion records that the action was prevented. Cancellation and command delivery share one admission check, so an expired request cannot queue a write later. After a command is queued, a lost result remains uncertain. Closing the browser connection still requires confirmed detach and transport cleanup.

The three files in `test-tls` are synthetic fixture material. The loopback fixture profile embeds `ca.pem`; the server certificate and server key are used only by tests. Public provider requests use their configured trust settings. None of these files grants access to a live service.

Browser button actions and single-select option choices use the existing saved approval and Chromiumoxide engine. Selection receipts report the exact option observed in the local DOM; they do not claim site persistence or form submission. Native button controls in the observed main document receive one bounded Chrome mouse gesture. Selection changes emit synthetic input and change events. Approval checks the task tab and exact document even when another tab is active. Changing tabs does not redirect the action. The button receipt uses the isolated automation world and reports an observed trusted click separately from site success. A page can move a control between the check and input. Missing or conflicting evidence after admission stays uncertain, and an effect may already have occurred. Button navigation does not adopt a new document grant.

Browser scrolling uses the same saved approval and Chromiumoxide engine. The page and nested regions have handles from the current observation. Receipts show the actual position after an instant request and a second read, including no movement. Changed targets and positions prevent dispatch. A lost admitted result is uncertain and is never replayed. Main document targets are supported; frame and shadow root scrolling remain unavailable.

# Harness registry

The one list of agent harnesses MetLDR drives: Pi, Codex, OpenCode and Claude Code. Each entry holds the stable wire key, the display label, the executable names to look for and the capabilities MetLDR may offer for it. The companion and the panel read names and capabilities from here instead of repeating them, so adding a harness is one entry here and one adapter in the companion.

`detect` finds each harness executable on `PATH` and in common user install folders, and where Claude Desktop, the Codex app, OpenCode and Cursor keep their MCP configuration, without running or changing anything. Claude Desktop has no Linux build and ChatGPT adds MCP servers in its own settings, so neither has a local file to find there.

`handoff::build` prepares the context a conversation carries when it moves to another harness or model: the newest items first under a character cap, page and tool text labelled untrusted, the covered runs and the count left out, and an instruction never to repeat earlier browser actions. It can send only what happened since the target last took part, or the whole conversation.

# metldr native credentials

This Rust crate stores provider keys for the native companion in the operating
system credential store. The caller owns provider selection and recovery of
interrupted settings changes.

`CredentialId::generate` creates a random scope or revision identifier.
`Vault::put`, `read` and `remove` operate on a revision within that scope.
`Key::parse` accepts 1 to 4096 ASCII graphic bytes. `Key` clears its owned
buffer when dropped and exposes its value only through `expose`.

Hold one process lock for the scope throughout writes and cleanup. The crate
serializes writes inside one process. Use a fresh revision identifier when a
key changes, and journal that identifier before writing. Existing identical
values are accepted; conflicting values return an error. Deletion is
idempotent. An interrupted partial write needs deliberate recovery by its caller.

Values use one or two bounded records. The head is written last and removed
first. Resolve a key before admitting work and keep that resolved value with
the run. Removing its vault record does not erase values already read into memory.

Linux uses an encrypted Secret Service session and requires an existing,
unlocked, persistent default collection. Missing or locked storage returns
an error. Windows uses Credential Manager. macOS uses Keychain.
The Windows and macOS backends still need runtime verification on those systems.

From the repository root, run `make check-credentials` for the ordinary checks.
Cargo remains available directly:

```sh
cargo fmt --manifest-path crates/metldr-native-credentials/Cargo.toml -- --check
cargo test --offline --locked --manifest-path crates/metldr-native-credentials/Cargo.toml
```

The ordinary checks validate inputs and record decoding without accessing a
credential store. The ignored Linux check requires the explicit owned fixture
marker and a separate Secret Service. It must never run against a personal store.

# Rust panel module

The crate implements the Chrome side panel and its background message handling in Rust and WebAssembly. It provides streamed results, retained assistant messages and tool activity, browser action decisions, provider and installed agent settings, cancellation and saved run restoration. Native work and saved run ownership stay with the paired companion. The normal extension build includes this panel at `panel.html`. The toolbar initially opens the existing page tools while their Rust migration continues.

Run `make check-panel` to check the Rust module. Run `make rust` to build the browser bindings and record the matching chat receipt. Both commands use the pinned Rust toolchain. The build also needs the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target and `wasm-bindgen-cli` version 0.2.128, matching the crate dependency. Set `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` to choose the Cargo build directory.

The generated `metldr_panel.js` exports `start_panel` and `accept_panel`. Initialize the generated module before calling its exports. The panel document must be `panel.html` within the same extension, with an `app` element and the expected browser event bindings. The background passes only its named connected extension ports to `accept_panel`. Other extension ports keep their existing owner. The small Chrome binding opens the selected panel directly from its command callback, preserving the required user gesture. The module validates the sender and owns the native connection to `io.metldr.first_flow` using wire version 19. A paired, registered companion and the extension permissions are required for native execution.

The UI bridge exposes `active_run()` after a fresh snapshot. Its handle observes the saved task through ordered events and stops only that task. The agent adapter uses `connectAgent()` to attach without submitting another request. Detaching a view releases its subscription while native work continues. Detach the agent and free the active handle when closing its view. Reconnecting requires a fresh handle. Update the extension and companion together.

`ui_bridge/run.rs` owns the shared run driver and delivers typed `Event` values to a Rust callback. `Core::stream` uses that callback for saved run updates. # rune-motion

Rune's animation runtime: springs, tweens, decay, keyframes, retargeting, presence and
transitions (blur-replace included), layout animation, matched geometry and choreography. It is
plain math and data structures with no renderer dependency and no required dependencies (the
optional `serde` feature covers the config types). App code states targets. The render thread
samples them once per frame and gets back what to draw.

```rust
use rune_motion::prelude::*;

let mut scene = Scene::new();
let card = NodeId(1);

// The first build never animates.
scene.insert(card, NodeSpec::new(Rect::new(0.0, 0.0, 320.0, 80.0)).radius(12.0), Mount::Initial);

// Later: a new row blurs in place, the card reflows with width leading, then something leaves.
let row = NodeId(2);
scene.insert(row, NodeSpec::new(Rect::new(0.0, 96.0, 320.0, 44.0))
    .parent(card)
    .transition(Transition::blur_replace()), Mount::Animated);
scene.set_frame(card, Rect::new(0.0, 0.0, 360.0, 160.0), LayoutAnim::new(motion::MORPH).width_leads());
scene.remove(NodeId(3));                       // stays drawn until its exit settles

let out = scene.frame_at(1.0 / 120.0);         // render thread, once per frame
for p in out.changed { /* draw p.rect, p.opacity, p.affine(), p.blur, p.mask … */ }
```

Without a scene graph, the store animates any property directly:

```rust
let mut store = AnimationStore::new();
store.set(id, prop::OPACITY, 0.0);
store.animate(id, prop::OPACITY, 1.0, motion::SETTLE);            // spring, bounce 0
store.animate(id, prop::FRAME, rect, motion::MORPH.delay(0.05));  // edges, delayed
store.animate(id, X, 40.0, Curve::ease_in_out(0.3).completion(7)); // tween, Completed{token: 7}
store.release(id, X, fling_v, Release::DecayClamped { decay: Decay::IOS_NORMAL, min: 0.0, max, spring: motion::SNAP });
store.tick_at(now);
let x = store.get(id, X);
```

## API overview

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Spring` | SwiftUI `Spring(duration:bounce:)`, bounce 0 by default, closed form in every damping regime. `sample`, `settling_duration`, `css_linear` (WAAPI export), plus constructors from response/damping fraction, ω/ζ, stiffness/damping/mass and Motion `visualDuration`. |
| `Curve` / `Anim` | `Spring`, `Tween` (CSS cubic-bezier, steps, linear), `Decay` (iOS rates), `Keyframes` (Hermite cubics that keep velocity across keys), `Instant`. `Anim` adds `.delay()`, `.additive()`/`.merge()`, `.velocity()` and `.completion(token)`. |
| `motion::*` tokens | `INSTANT SNAP SETTLE REFLOW GLIDE MORPH POP DRIFT CAMERA`, each with an `_EXIT` partner 10–25 % shorter (copied from Kit's motion presets), plus `motion::pair::*` `SpringPair`s and SwiftUI presets. |
| `Animatable` | `f32`, `Vec2`, `Rect` (four edges), `Color` (premultiplied OKLab), `Corners`, `Sides`, `Transform`, `Blur`, tuples and arrays. Up to `MAX_LANES` f32 lanes. |
| `AnimationStore` | Every animated value is a track. Retargeting keeps position and velocity. Also delays, settle and completion events, gesture `release` (spring, decay, decay-into-bounds), `retune` for live token edits, and reduced motion per `PropClass`. |
| `Scene` | Keyed nodes with presence (exits stay mounted, revive mid-exit without a jump), `Transition`s (`opacity scale offset move push slide blur_replace reveal asymmetric combined`), layout by edges (`Travel::Parent`) or one straight screen path (`Travel::Screen`), `match_geometry`, popLayout. |
| Choreography | `Choreography` steps cue on `Cue::now/at/started/arrived/settled(step).after(s).not_before(t)`. Also `Stagger` (from start, end, centre or an index, eased), `PhaseAnimator` and `Keyframes`. |
| Gestures | `VelocityTracker`, `project`, `rubber_band*`, `deceleration`. |
| `Animated<T>` | A single value outside any store, for one-off widgets. |
| `Clock` | A display clock with pause, scale and seek, or a manual clock for tests and offline renders. |
| `LoopTrack` / `LoopSpec` | Periodic eased opacity or clockwise rotation, sampled at clock time. `retime` preserves phase; `enabled` springs the pulse amplitude toward rest. The renderer owns visibility and scheduling. |
| `MotionTrace` | motion-trace JSONL. `MotionTrace::from_env` opens `$RUNE_MOTION_TRACE`. |

### Kit's motion rules are the defaults

- Springs are duration plus bounce, with bounce 0 by default. Exits run 10–25 % shorter than entrances.
- Interrupting a motion keeps its position and velocity.
- Nothing animates on first mount. A track's first `animate` acts as `set`, and setting an unchanged target does nothing.
- The user's direct manipulation is never animated. Gestures write values with `set` and animate only on `release`.
- Under reduced motion, travel, scale, shape and blur change instantly, and opacity, colour and presence take a 0.18 s ease-in-out fade (`REDUCED_FADE`). Gesture values keep their curve. `match_geometry` turns into a crossfade in place.
- Both edges of a rect snap to 1/64 device px, and settle thresholds scale with the pixel density.
- Blur is limited to 4 px and only applies to things entering or leaving in place. A transition that travels drops its blur. Scale stays within [0.9, 1.1] and never goes to 0; `Transition::allow_small_scale()` lowers the floor to 0.5 for small glyphs. A removed node always fades out (`Effect::kit_rules`).
- Width leads: `.width_leads()` runs the X spring at 0.78× the duration (taken from a launcher app).
- A stationary edge gets no motion at all.
- A node given `Scene::set_ride_trailing` keeps its place against its parent's trailing edge while the parent's width animates; its frame is still given in parent space.

## Design

**Analytic tracks.** Each value lane is `target + Σ offset layers`. A layer is a closed-form
segment: an underdamped, critical or overdamped spring, a decay, a tween or a Hermite cubic. Each
one is evaluated directly at the frame's timestamp. Nothing is integrated step by step, so
results are the same at any frame rate. Sampling at the display link's *target* timestamp is
exact, frames can be skipped, and tests can jump to any `t`. Each layer stores its own settle
time, an upper bound that holds for the whole tail (spring envelopes, or bisection for the
critical and overdamped cases). Once that time passes, the track snaps to `(target, 0)`, leaves
the active list and costs nothing.

**Merge vs additive.** Springs, decay and keyframes *merge* by default: the store samples
`(x, v)` and starts one new segment from there, like SwiftUI spring merging or Compose
`animateTo`. That keeps one layer per lane and O(1) sampling. Tweens *add* by default, Core
Animation style: the running curves continue, and a new layer animates the target delta to 0, so
every curve keeps its shape. A test checks that additive springs give exactly the same result as
merged springs. A lane holds at most 8 additive layers. Past that, they collapse into one merged
segment.

**Struct of arrays.** Track data lives in flat lane arrays (layer, target, value, velocity), with
generational `TrackId`s, a dense `active` list, free-list pools for extra layers and delayed
starts, and an Fx-style hash map from `(node, prop)` to track. A tick walks only the active
tracks, reads contiguous memory and does not allocate. `tests/alloc.rs` checks this with a
counting allocator.

**Deterministic math.** `math::exp` and `math::sin_cos` are custom polynomial versions (Estrin's
scheme, FMA on aarch64 or `+fma`, branchless quadrant fix-up). They don't depend on the
platform's libm, so traces and goldens stay stable, and they're cheap: 5 ns for `exp` and 7.6 ns
for `sin_cos`.

**Presence.** One `PRESENCE` progress (0 means absent, 1 means present) drives the insertion and
removal effects. If a node is reversed mid-flight (it comes back while exiting, or leaves while
entering), the effect endpoints are re-solved at the current visual state so nothing jumps.
`Travel::Screen` interpolates root-space start and end edges with a separate progress per axis.
`match_geometry` starts the target node at the source's exact presented rect, velocity, radius
and fill, then removes the source immediately.

## Renderer integration contract

Run this on the render thread once per display-link callback:

1. `scene.set_time(target_timestamp)`. Use the timestamp the frame will be *shown* at, not the
   current time. `Clock::frame(host)` handles pause, slow motion and seek.
2. Apply the commits that arrived since the last frame: `insert(id, spec, mount)`, `remove(id)`,
   `set_frame(id, rect, anim)`, `animate(id, prop, target, anim)`, `set(...)` and
   `match_geometry(from, to, anim)`. Pass `Mount::Initial` for the first build.
3. `let out = scene.frame()`, which returns a `FrameOutput`:
   - `changed: &[Presented]`: only the nodes whose presented values changed, parents before
     children.
   - `exited: &[NodeId]`: nodes whose exit settled. Stop drawing them and free their resources.
   - `events: &[MotionEvent]`: `Settled` and `Completed { token, finished }`, for app callbacks.
   - `animating: bool`: when false, pause the display link until the next commit.

`Presented` holds everything needed to draw one node:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `rect` | Root-space rect. It already includes every ancestor's translation and this node's own, and both edges are snapped to 1/64 device px. Draw shapes, borders and shadows at this size. |
| `opacity` | This node's own opacity (presence × property). Apply ancestors' opacity as group opacity. |
| `transform`, `anchor` | Scale and rotation about the root-space `anchor`, composed down the tree like `CALayer`. `affine()` returns the 2×3 matrix. |
| `blur` | Own plus presence Gaussian sigma in points. 0 means attach no filter. Presence effects clamp to ≤ 4 pt; `blur_replace` peaks at 1.5 pt. Explicit property blur can remain at rest. |
| `radius`, `fill` | Animated corner radii, and the fill as sRGB with straight alpha (interpolated in premultiplied OKLab). |
| `mask` | `Mask { inset: Sides, feather: Sides }` in the node's own coordinates: how far each side is pulled in, and the gradient width on that side. Evaluate it as an SDF ramp. `mask.is_none()` means no clip. |
| `phase` | `Entering`, `Present` or `Exiting { generation }`. |
| `in_flow` | Turns false as soon as a popLayout exit starts. App layout should stop reserving space for the node. |
| `flags` | motion-trace bits (`flags::ANIMATED`, `ANCESTOR_ANIMATED`, `CLIPPED`, `FILTERED`) and intent bits (own `<< 8`, ancestor `<< 16`). |

Call `scene.set_pixel_scale(scale)` on display changes and `scene.set_reduced_motion(on)` when the
system setting changes. Setting `RUNE_MOTION_TRACE=/path.jsonl` and calling
`scene.set_trace(MotionTrace::from_env(&header))` writes motion traces.

# rune

Rune's core crate: views, layout, animation, rendering, text and the native shell.
`examples/settings` draws a small Settings window entirely with Rune's own code.

![dark](../../demo/settings-dark.png)

## What exists

- **View API** (`el.rs`): `fn view(s: &S, cx: &mut Cx<S>) -> El`, with `row()/col()/el()/text()`,
  `.key(..)`, layout and style methods, `.on_press(|s: &mut S| ..)`, `.on_press_tx(|s, tx| ..)` and
  `.on_drag(|s, drag, tx| ..)`. Handlers are queued and run between frames with `&mut S`. Then the view
  re-runs, and the diff retargets property tracks. Hover and press only retarget tracks; they never
  re-run the view.
- **Tokens** (`tok.rs`): colours in OKLCH (dark and light themes, six accents), plus space, radius, type
  and the motion palette (snappy .25/0, default .3/0, calm .4/0, a .2/0 lead, a .15 fade).
- **Layout**: Taffy 0.15 at the target state. Text sizes round up to whole device pixels, so layout
  stays on the pixel grid. Keyed nodes retain Taffy's constraint cache between commits; only changed
  styles, children or text measurements dirty it. Text colour does not invalidate measurement.
  Three gotchas, all CSS flexbox behaviour:
  - `.grow(g)` is `flex: g 1 0`: flex-basis 0, so the element is only as big as the free space its
    parent leaves. In an auto-height column there is none, and a grown `.scroll(..)` viewport
    collapses to 0 pt. Bound an ancestor's height (`.h(..)`, `.h_full()`) or set `.min_h(..)`.
  - Flex items default to a minimum of their content size, so a nested flex column overflows its
    parent instead of shrinking and the scroll inside never scrolls. Put `.min_h(0.0)` on each
    column between the bounded ancestor and the viewport.
  - `.virtualize(..)` only works on a growth stack: call `.growth(GrowthSpec)` on the same element,
    and make it the scroll viewport's first child.

  Debug builds warn once per call site when a scroll viewport inside a `.grow()` container
  resolves to 0 pt while its content is taller; `.virtualize` without `.growth` panics with the
  element's path.
- **Animation** (`rune-motion`, `runtime.rs`): analytic springs (`Spring::new(duration, bounce)`),
  tweens, decay and transitions driven through `rune_motion::Scene` and `AnimationStore`. Retargets
  keep exact position and velocity.
  - Layout animates per edge, so stationary edges never move.
  - `.lead(lead, trail)` makes the edge in the direction of travel lead; `.width_leads()` speeds up X
    by `0.78×`.
  - Children ride their parent's left edge. `.ride_trailing()` keeps an element against its parent's
    right edge instead while the parent's width animates, so right-aligned content holds still
    whatever springs the rows around it use (a trailing `RollingText` does this).
  - Presence (`Transition`): elements added or removed after the first frame animate in and stay drawn
    until their exit settles at opacity 0 (including `.transition(Transition::blur_replace())` and
    mid-flight revival).
  - Colours animate in premultiplied OKLab, and text colour leads its background (`0.5×` duration) so
    theme switches keep label contrast through the transition.
  - Nothing animates on the first frame.
  - `Tx::instant()` applies a change with no animation (drag moves are instant by default).
  - `El::instant_changes()` does the same for one subtree in any commit (a popup of search results),
    while the element's own entrance and exit and its colours keep their motion.
  - `Tx::color_motion(spring)` sets the spring for that change's colours (the theme switch uses calm).
  - In reduced motion, spatial travel snaps while opacity, presence and colour take `REDUCED_FADE`
    (`0.15 s`). Growth-stack rows also keep this fade on insertion/removal; closing gaps land after
    the exit fade instead of animating their height.
  - The animation clock has a time scale, which the Settings speed slider drives.
- **Renderer** (`render.rs`, `shader.wgsl`): one instanced uber-quad pipeline and one draw call per
  frame.
  - Kinds: rounded rects (per-corner radius, border), analytic Gaussian shadows (outer and inset),
    vertical and angled linear gradients, circular and elliptical radial gradients (`KIND_RADIAL`),
    dashed border rings (`KIND_DASHED`), RGBA images, and glyphs from the atlas.
  - **Gradients** (`.gradient(top, bottom)`, `.radial_gradient(center, radius, stops)`,
    `.linear_gradient(angle, stops)`): painted over `.fill(..)` and under hover/press overlays and
    borders, clipped to `.radius(..)`, and composited with `.opacity(..)` and `.blur(..)`.
    `radial_gradient` takes normalized `center: [f32; 2]` (`[0.5, 0.5]` = element centre), `radius` in
    points (`f32` for a circle or `[rx, ry]` for an ellipse), and up to 8 `stops` as `(t, Color)` pairs in
    `0.0..=1.0` (inner radial bands shrink their quads to the band bounding box). `linear_gradient`
    takes `angle` in radians (CSS convention: `0.0` up, `PI / 2` right, `PI` down) and up to 8 `stops`.
    Stop colours spring in Oklab when changed and interpolate in premultiplied colour across the quad.
  - **Shadows** (`.shadow(y, blur, color)`, `.box_shadow(Shadow)`): `blur` follows CSS `box-shadow`
    (`blur = 2σ`, so the Gaussian standard deviation is `σ = blur * 0.5`). `CALayer.shadowRadius` and
    Sketch / Figma shadow blur specify `r ≈ σ`, so pass `blur = 2.0 * r` to match a `CALayer` shadow
    radius (whereas `.blur(sigma)` takes `σ` directly).
  - Vector shapes (`shape.rs`): `El::shape(Shape)` and `canvas(shape)` paint strokes (polylines,
    round or butt caps, open or closed) and fills (simple polygons, ear-clipped) in the element's own
    points, or in a `view_box` stretched to the element's size; `Path` flattens quadratic and cubic
    Béziers. Strokes are one analytic capsule/box per
    segment (`KIND_SEGMENT`); fills are triangles (`KIND_TRIANGLE`) antialiased only on polygon
    edges, so they have no seams. No atlas, so a shape can change every frame (`examples/shapes`).
    Translucent strokes blend twice where segments overlap at a joint; fills do not overlap.
  - Every instance has a soft-edge clip (`clip_soft`, `clip_fade`).
  - Windows blend in sRGB-encoded space by default, as Core Animation, CoreText and CSS do.
    `.srgb_blend(false)` on `App`, `WindowSpec` or `ConfiguredOverlay` opts out into linear-light
    blending (colour premultiplied in linear light, drawn into an sRGB target). sRGB blending
    encodes premultiplied colours in sRGB (`Color::premul_srgb`) and renders into a non-sRGB
    target view (`format.remove_srgb_suffix()`). With a `Compositor`, `Frame::srgb_blend()` and `Frame::format` tell it which encoding and view its own passes must match.
    A runtime the app draws itself (`Runtime::with_text`, a headless snapshot) opts in with
    `Runtime::set_srgb_blend(true)`, then draws with `Renderer::set_srgb_blend(true)` into a
    non-sRGB target cleared to `clear_color()`; hover and press tints follow the mode.
    A handler switches a running window with `Tx::set_srgb_blend(bool)`: the frame that switches
    reconfigures the surface and rebuilds the renderer once (the web canvas keeps its format and
    changes its view).
  - The Retina scale is applied throughout.
- **Text** (`text.rs`): Parley 0.12 lays out embedded Inter 4.1 (OFL, `assets/`). swash 0.2
  outlines are rasterised through a port of CoreGraphics' glyph pipeline into a 2048² R8 shelf
  atlas, at CoreGraphics' subpixel pen steps, with a 1 px zeroed border per glyph and
  pixel-snapped baselines.
  **Font smoothing** (`FontSmoothing`, `text/coretext_match.rs`) picks how glyphs are rasterised

### Compatible edits and restart boundaries

The launcher validates Rust syntax, then copies compatible edits into a private compiler
mirror. It accepts function-body changes in Settings' `main.rs`. Use stable keys to preserve node identity.

**Restart needed** is printed before publishing changes to state/type declarations,
function signatures, imports, constants, const-fn bodies, impl methods, startup code, dependencies,
assets or framework code. This catches same-size field/type changes too; `size_of`
alone cannot. Syntax errors stay outside the mirror until fixed. Stop and rerun the
command after an incompatible change (`--local` and `scripts/rune-hot` rebuild and relaunch
on their own). State is not migrated across restarts.
Function attributes other than `doc`, `inline`, `cold` and `allow` also keep the whole
body in the restart contract, since attribute macros can generate persistent types.

Keep persistent state in `AppSpec::init`'s returned value. Tip-crate statics and thread
locals can reset after any patch; use them only for disposable caches. Do not retain
view-owned trait objects in app state. Rune replaces its event-handler trait objects
at the patch boundary. Arbitrary cached vtables, background callbacks and initializer
edits do not hot-reload. Use this launcher, not raw `dx serve`, to keep the source guard.
`poll` and `on_key` go through the patch table each call, like the view. `setup` runs once
at startup, so edits to it, and to helpers only it calls, take effect after a restart.

If a patched view panics, in any window or overlay, Rune logs it and renders the
original startup view against the retained state, discarding the failed view's context
changes and memo cache. A panicking patched `poll` or `on_key` falls back to the startup
callback the same way, keeping whatever it changed before the panic. A later patch is
still attempted. Handler-closure panics are not caught; neither are panics in the
original fallbacks. This recovery requires Rust's unwinding panic mode and does
not undo interior-mutability side effects performed by a view before it panics.
Physical iOS devices are unsupported by this backend.

`--snap-on-patch` keeps one offscreen renderer alive. It publishes the initial PNG/tree
and another after each patch or control request, then flushes `rune-hot-pixels` with the
patch generation, PID, state address, scroll offsets and GPU-readback timestamp.
The PNG is the first patched frame; animated properties may still be near their old
values. The renderer continues advancing normal animation time between edits.

Replace the `--hot-control` JSON file atomically to send a request. Give each request

Each line above is a separate file replacement. `pause` freezes the virtual clock;

# Global shortcuts

```rust,ignore
let app = App::new(spec)
    .global_shortcut("cmd+shift+space", |state, tx| {
        state.quick_panel_open = true;
        if let Some(token) = tx.activation_token() {
            state.app_handle.activate(token);
        } else {
            state.app_handle.open();
        }
    })
    .windowless();
app.run();
```

The handler receives the same state as its `App`/`WindowSpec`, on the app thread.
It runs through `Runtime::update`, including animation and shell requests. Native
activation wakes the loop even while no window is visible.

Static builder failures print once and can be drained with
`handle.take_shortcut_errors()`. The builder defers registration until the app's
host exists, so `run_windows_with` factories can construct apps normally.

Runtime registration returns the actual result:

```rust,ignore
let id = handle.register_shortcut("ctrl+alt+k".parse()?, |state, tx| {
    state.open_quick_panel(tx.activation_token());
})?;
handle.unregister_shortcut(id)?;
```

After a `Conflict`, `handle.shortcut_owner(&shortcut)` names the holder when Rune or
the desktop knows it: this App or another Rune App in the process (its `AppSpec`
title), or a macOS system shortcut ("Spotlight", "Mission Control", "Input Sources",
"Screenshot", "App Switcher", "macOS" for other enabled symbolic hotkeys), at the chord
the user remapped it to. The macOS lookup answers only on the main thread. A chord
another Rune App in the process holds is refused with `Conflict` on every backend. Other apps'
grabs, Windows, X11 and the portal name nobody, so it returns None. Headless runs
answer only for their own virtual registrations. `ShortcutError::Conflict` itself is
unchanged.

A chord needs ⌘, ⌃ or ⌥ (Ctrl, Alt or Super elsewhere), or an F1–F24 key, because a
global Space or ⇧A would take that key from typing in every app. Both the builder and
`register_shortcut` refuse one without them with `InvalidAccelerator`
(`shortcut.require_modifier()` checks it), unless the App opts in with
`.allow_unmodified_shortcuts()`.

Call runtime registration after the host starts (an `on_window` or queued
`handle.update` callback works, including one on another window of the same
`run_windows`). Calls before startup or after shutdown return `NotRunning`. On macOS/Windows other threads may call it, but wait for the app
thread, so the app thread must not join those callers. Linux registration can
run off-thread. Dropping the host unregisters everything,
even if other threads retain `AppHandle`s.

## Desktop behavior

- macOS: Carbon `RegisterEventHotKey`, no Accessibility permission. Command is
  the Super modifier. Hardware key positions follow the US layout; F21–F24 have
  no Carbon key code and return `InvalidAccelerator`.
- Windows: `RegisterHotKey` on a message-only window owned by the event thread.
  Repeat is disabled. Windows-reserved combinations may fail registration.
- X11: checked passive grabs on every root, including CapsLock/NumLock variants.
  A failed variant rolls back the registration. Autorepeat is filtered, so a held
  chord fires once, as on macOS and Windows. Keys use the current keymap's
  base keysyms; restart/re-register after changing the keymap.
- Wayland: xdg-desktop-portal GlobalShortcuts. No portal returns `Unsupported`.
  The portal may ask for permission or let the user choose another trigger;
  `preferred_trigger` is a preference, not an exclusive-grab guarantee. Cancellation
  is `PermissionDenied`, not `Conflict`. Each shortcut owns a portal session so
  unregister also works with version 1. The activation token is available only
  during its handler, through `Tx::activation_token()`.

Registration is synchronous, including portal consent, with a two-minute bound.
Register startup shortcuts before showing windows; use a worker thread for
runtime Wayland binding so a consent dialog does not block the event thread.

Only an actual registration creates native resources: macOS/Windows need no
listener thread; X11/Wayland each create a listener that is joined on teardown.
No-shortcut apps never open a shortcut display or portal connection.

### Standard menus

`App::standard_menus()` adds an Edit menu (Undo ⌘Z, Redo ⇧⌘Z, Cut ⌘X, Copy ⌘C, Paste
⌘V, Select All ⌘A) and a Window menu (Minimize ⌘M, Close ⌘W) to the process menu bar
when the first window of that App starts. A regular (non-accessory) app gets the same
items without asking, as long as its menu bar is still winit's default when its first
window starts; an app that set its own menu bar is left alone. Rune never adds Quit:
an accessory app that later shows its Dock icon gets winit's app menu (with Quit) as
before. Items go into existing menus of the same title, an item whose action is
already there is skipped, and custom `MenuItem`s keep working in either order. A
custom item with a standard item's equivalent (Close Tab ⌘W) takes it: the standard
item shows none until the custom one goes, whichever was set first. New custom menus
take the Mac order: File before Edit, the app's other menus before Window, Help last.
Clearing custom items keeps a menu the standard items share. An accessory app's menu
bar is hidden, but AppKit still matches its key equivalents.

Every item has a nil target, so AppKit sends it to the key window's first responder:

- An AppKit window in the process (an open panel, an updater's window) gets the
  normal `copy:`, `paste:`, `selectAll:`, `undo:`, `performMiniaturize:` and
  `performClose:` of its focused field or window.
- A Rune window's first responder is winit's view. AppKit consumes a matched key
  equivalent even when no responder implements its action, which is why a plain Edit
  menu would swallow ⌘C before Rune sees it. So the view gains the eight actions (added
  to winit's view class, never replacing a method it has), and each hands Rune the key:
  the very event that fired the item, so text fields, `on_key` and shortcuts see exactly
  the `Key::Command` they did without the menu, once. A click on the item sends a
  made-up press and release of its key instead.
- An IME composition (or a dead key's accent) in the focused field ends first, as in an
  NSTextView: the input method commits it into the field, then the command acts. One
  that doesn't commit is dropped, so the key still reaches Rune.
- ⌘W and ⌘M reach Rune the same way first. If no handler takes them and the window has
  that title-bar button, the window then closes or minimizes as a click on the button
  would: `on_close` and `keep_running` hiding apply. A window without the button
  (borderless, an overlay or nonactivating panel) only gets the key. An app that binds ⌘W itself keeps it.

Without `standard_menus`, an accessory app's keys don't change.

Native Windows/Linux return `MenuError::Unsupported`; startup builders report it
through `take_menu_errors()`. Headless virtual menus work on every platform:
`{"menu":"Open Quick Panel"}` invokes by exact id or unambiguous title. Unknown,
disabled and ambiguous items fail the script.

`scripts/check-native-menu-macos.py <menu_probe>` exercises the app-menu click,
key equivalent, named-menu click, runtime enabled/checked updates, preservation of
Quit/Hide and the Dock delegate selector on a GUI test Mac, under the same lock.
`scripts/check-dock-menu-macos.py <dock_menu_probe>` checks the accessory-to-Regular
default menu in both orders. `scripts/menu.json` exercises title/id dispatch headlessly.

# Element Scouts

Status: proposal. This document describes a fast, element-scoped decision layer for the browser agent. It does not describe shipped behavior.

## Summary

Element Scouts change where the browser agent spends its model budget. Instead of sending a whole page to a planner on every step, the agent extracts a bounded set of candidates (links, fields, buttons, result rows), asks a fast structured-decision model to rank them against the current subgoal, and gives the planner a compact shortlist.

The first candidate provider is [Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev), TypeSafe's System One model. Jev accepts typed questions and returns typed answers with full probability distributions and calibrated confidence in roughly 70–500 ms. It does not generate strings. A local fallback using the bundled embedding model keeps the feature usable offline and on privacy-sensitive pages.

The planner still decomposes goals, resolves ambiguity, recovers from failure and writes the final answer. Scouts only decide which element is the next step.

## Problem

The current loop is planner-centric. On every step the agent observes the page and sends page text, controls and history to a capable model, then waits for a generated action. That has four costs.

1. **Latency.** Frontier API responses range from seconds to minutes. A local 7B model is also slow per step. Multi-step tasks compound the delay.
2. **CPU and GPU pressure.** Local generative inference is expensive. An embedding or classification pass is one to two orders of magnitude cheaper.
3. **Context dilution.** The relevant link is one line among thousands of tokens. Large models reliably miss items in long context, especially in the middle.
4. **Per-step reliability.** Multi-step success multiplies. Ten steps at 90% per step is about 35% task success; ten steps at 97% is about 74%. Small per-step gains matter enormously.

Most browsing steps are not open-ended reasoning. They are closed-set decisions inside a page: which link, which field, which result row, whether the answer is already here. That is the shape a System One model is built for.

## Why Jev

Jev is not a small local LLM. It is a hosted model that evaluates typed questions against a state and returns typed answers. Relevant properties:

- **Question types.** `Choice` selects one option from up to 255. `Score` places the state on an ordered rubric. `Noul` returns the probability that a statement is true. `Box` locates a region in an image.
- **Speed.** TypeSafe reports 70–500 ms end to end, with questions evaluated in parallel.
- **Cost.** $0.042 per million input tokens; output tokens are free. A 3k-token page decision costs roughly $0.0001.
- **Type safety.** Outputs are typed, so the model cannot emit a malformed handle or tool call. It can still choose the wrong option; confidence is the mitigation.
- **Confidence.** Every `Choice` and `Score` answer includes probabilities and a confidence value. This enables a confidence-gated escalation policy.
- **No strings.** It cannot plan, summarize, draft or explain. It decides; the planner narrates and strategizes.

TypeSafe's Wikiracing demo is direct evidence for the link-selection case: choose among hundreds to thousands of links per step, and Jev finished in fewer steps than the LLMs.

The public API is hosted. It is not a local or offline model, and enterprise VPC or on-premises deployment is a separate agreement. The design therefore keeps a local fallback and requires explicit consent before page content leaves the device.

## Design

### Candidate extraction

The observer currently captures page text, text fields, buttons, selects, native controls and scroll targets. It does not capture links. Element Scouts need links first.

Add a `links` array to observation with:

- an opaque handle in the existing identifier format;
- bounded visible text;
- an `href`, normalized and checked against the navigation policy;
- nearby context (heading or landmark);
- visibility and same-origin flags.

The candidate budget is about 150 visible, deduplicated entries. Hidden nodes, sensitive fields and non-HTTP(S) destinations are excluded. Handles remain opaque and bounded, and are resolved against the latest observation.

### Decision provider

Introduce a `DecisionProvider` boundary with two implementations:

- `JevDecisionProvider` calls `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with `model: "jev-latest"`.
- `LocalDecisionProvider` uses the existing sandbox or offscreen stack: the bundled embedding model for ranking, the zero-shot classifier for roles, and BERT-NER for entities.

The provider is selected per session with an explicit fallback. The API key stays in the Rust companion, consistent with existing provider key handling. Page content is only sent after consent.

### `scout_page`

Add a read-only tool beside `observe_page`.

Input:

```json
{
  "subgoal": "find the faculty directory",
  "kinds": ["link", "button", "field"],
  "limit": 12
}
```

Output:

```json
{
  "url": "https://example.edu/",
  "title": "Example University",
  "candidates": [
    {
      "handle": "link_12",
      "kind": "link",
      "text": "Faculty Directory",
      "href": "/faculty",
      "context": "Academics",
      "score": 0.91,
      "role": "directory",
      "confidence": 0.88
    }
  ],
  "page_type": "directory",
  "answer_present": 0.04,
  "injection_risk": 0.02
}
```

Scouting is advisory and read-only. It grants no new authority. The agent still acts through the existing approval-gated tools using handles from the latest observation.

### Jev question schema

One request per observation, with several questions evaluated in parallel:

| Question id | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `next_element` | `Choice` | Rank candidates against the subgoal |
| `page_type` | `Choice` | directory, search, results, profile, article, other |
| `answer_present` | `Noul` | Is the answer already on this page? |
| `injection_risk` | `Noul` | Does the page try to instruct the agent? |

The `Choice` probabilities provide a full ranking, not just a top-1 pick. The shortlist builder sorts them and applies role and region diversity.

Choice supports up to 255 options. For larger pages, prefilter locally to 255. If still larger, score candidates in batches and run a final choice on the top slice.

### Confidence gate

Thresholds are placeholders until the benchmark calibrates them.

| Confidence | Behavior |
|---|---|
| High (top probability at least 0.75, clear margin) | Execute the action |
| Medium (0.4 to 0.75) | Planner chooses from the top-k shortlist |
| Low (below 0.4) | Ask the user, scroll or re-observe; do not guess |

Thresholds scale with risk. Read-only navigation can act at a lower threshold than a form submission.

### Execution and verification

Scouts never execute. The planner selects an action, the existing approval flow runs, and the browser worker re-observes after dispatch. Handles from an earlier observation are invalid.

Emails, names, prices and other literal values are extracted from the DOM and cited. They are never generated by a scout or a planner. A verification question may check that an extracted value belongs to the named person, but the value itself comes from the page.

## Flow

```
goal
  → planner emits a local subgoal
  → observe page → candidates
  → scout_page (Jev or local)
  → probabilities + confidence
  → confidence gate
      high   → execute
      medium → planner picks from top-k
      low    → ask or re-observe
  → execute → re-observe → repeat
  → answer + citation
```

## Evaluation

Three configurations on the same benchmark:

| Config | Planner | Page input |
|---|---|---|
| A (baseline) | Capable LLM | Full observation |
| B (Jev scouts) | Capable LLM | `scout_page` shortlist |
| C (local scouts) | Capable LLM | Local shortlist |

Metrics: task success, answer correctness, citation correctness, steps, planner input tokens, wall-clock latency, CPU time, API cost, approval count, false-action rate and injection detection.

Benchmark: 12 goals across 5 site types (university directory, documentation, government, e-commerce, news), 3 runs each, with saved fixtures where possible. The proctor-email task is one seed case, not the benchmark.

Hypotheses:

- **H1:** B cuts planner input tokens by at least 80% versus A.
- **H2:** B matches or beats A on task success and is at least 2× faster at the median.
- **H3:** C is competitive on narrow tasks but loses on ambiguous, multi-page tasks.
- **H4:** The confidence gate reduces false actions versus always acting on the top choice.

## Risks

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Page content leaves the device | Explicit consent, visible indicator, per-site allowlist, local fallback |
| Prompt injection in page text | Treat page text as data; add an injection `Noul`; keep `BROWSER_POLICY` |
| Wrong confident choice | Calibrate thresholds per site; verify before irreversible actions |
| Vendor lock-in or early-access API changes | `DecisionProvider` boundary; pin the model version; contract tests |
| Network latency or outage | Timeout and fall back to local scouts |
| Cost at scale | Per-session budget caps; cache decisions by content hash |
| Over-trust in confidence | Confidence is not correctness; combine with deterministic verification |
| Dynamic DOM or single-page apps | Re-observe after every action; invalidate handles |
| Frames and shadow DOM | Known gap; `Box` on screenshots is a later fallback |

# Rune source

Source: https://github.com/anomalyco/rune
Revision: 781e2b6d87cd5f32d6f4365956fad4baaf24ee50

This directory keeps the Rune runtime, motion, staging, layout and optional profiling crates with their original relative paths. The workspace lists these crates and retains the upstream edition, license and lint settings. Dependency versions are owned by the consuming crate lockfile.

Local changes:

* The browser calls the existing frame-drawn hook after presentation, allowing restricted answer frames to follow submitted canvas geometry.
* Application fallback fonts are registered for Hebrew, Arabic, Devanagari, Bengali and Thai as well as CJK. Browser symbol fallback recognizes the supplied Noto Sans Symbols 2 family.
* The WebAssembly GPU instance cache uses thread local storage; native targets retain the upstream mutex.
* Browser field semantics share Rust paths and focus state with the existing text service bridge. Secure field values are omitted from the semantic mirror.
* Disabled fields cannot take focus through traversal or restoration, or retain offscreen editing focus.
* Text test fixtures use the identical font already bundled in the runtime.
* Focus and semantic mirror regressions cover these changes.
* A composition whose end event is refused as untrusted is finished by the next trusted input or key that is no longer composing, so the field never stays in a preedit. Mirror nodes rewrite their style only when it changes.
* `El::my_auto` sets auto top and bottom margins, so a centred column in a scroll viewport keeps its top reachable when it overflows.
* On the web every keyed control with a press handler takes the native mirror button path for focus and keyboard or assistive activation, not only controls marked `native_activation`; pointer presses on the canvas are unchanged. A focused mirror button forwards Tab, Escape, the arrows, Home, End, Page Up and Page Down to the runtime, and a held Enter or Space does not repeat the press.
* A touch holds the focus change its press asked for until the finger lifts, and drops it when the touch turns into a pan, as a browser focuses only on a tap. A scroll step after the press is cancelled skips the press search.
* The web mirror gives each pressable control its ARIA role (checkbox, switch, radio, menu item, tab, option, tree item) and state (pressed, checked, selected, disabled, busy), and `El::busy` marks a control whose action is still running. Mirror attributes are rewritten only when they change.
* `El::unavailable` marks a control that reads as disabled yet keeps focus and its place in the tab order (ARIA `aria-disabled`), in the web mirror and the native tree; the native tree also reports busy.
* Focus groups take `El::focus_axis` and `El::focus_wrap` in place of their role's arrows and wrapping, and Tab returns to the item in a group that last had focus.
* `El::has_popup` names the kind of popup a control opens (ARIA `aria-haspopup`), on the web mirror.
* `El::press_travel` sinks a control while it is pressed and keeps its outer shadows in place, so a key comes down onto its lip.
* The web host tracks effect marks when a compositor is attached, as the native window does, so compositor effect slots draw in the browser.
* `El::caret_block` draws a text field's caret as a block the width of the character after it (a space wide at a line end), as CSS `caret-shape: block`; that character takes the given ink, and a selection or composition hides the block (`tests/caret_block.rs`).
* `El::on_press_down` runs as a primary pointer press lands on an enabled element, before the release activates it, so a key can sound its down-stroke (`tests/press_down.rs`).
* On the web the hidden text field reports the keys it types and every key it releases as physical input, so a focused field's `El::on_physical_input` hears typing as it does on a native host; the password field reports none.
* `El::focus_ring_default` sets the default keyboard focus ring for every control inside an element that sets none of its own, so a theme draws its ring once at its root (`tests/focus_ring_default.rs`). Painting checks an element's own ring before walking up to the focus, so elements without one skip the walk.
* Web input stops untrusted (`isTrusted` false) input types in the window capture phase, before the page's listeners and winit's. Mirror presses and focus name the browser's trust and the mirror revision they were rendered from, and the runtime refuses any other (`runtime/input/provenance.rs`).
